Neuron vs vector browser

Neuron edit vs steering vector

How to read this page

Banked outputs from Qwen3 models with one MLP neuron pushed (left) or a distilled persona vector added to the residual stream (right). Each slider walks that method's Pareto frontier of behaviour against generic quality, from unsteered (0) to the frontier point with the most behaviour (5).

Pick a model and a behaviour, then move either slider. The plot marks each slider's position on its frontier, with a dashed ring at the measured means for that level.

Behaviour: trait judge score, 0–10. Generic quality: mean of HelpSteer2 helpfulness, correctness and coherence, rescaled to 0–10. Both from gpt-5.4-mini. Frontier points are means over the sweep prompts (50 for Qwen3-8B, 30 for Qwen3-32B); each slider level shows one sample on each of the same 8 prompts, so its measured means are noisy. Levels 1–4 sit at equal arc length along the frontier in (quality, behaviour), with dose interpolated linearly. Sampling: temperature 0.7, 200 new tokens.

Can a documented neuron work as a detector? Each detector is fitted only on 1,000 judge-labelled FineWeb passages (positive = judge score of 5 or more on the passage version of the rubric), then tested on simulated chats.

Simulated chats: gpt-5.4-mini plays a user whose opener invites the behaviour (Elicit), sits on a related topic that should not produce it (Near-miss), or asks for something unrelated (Generic). The model replies (up to 256 tokens; half of the Elicit chats get a second user turn and reply), and the judge labels every reply with the rubric shown.

Neuron score: the neuron's signed activation pooled over the reply tokens (max or mean, chosen on FineWeb). Probe score: an L2 logistic regression on the pooled, unit-normalised residual stream at the neuron's layer.

The chart shows simulated-chat AUROC as the probe gets 2 to 256 balanced FineWeb labels (20 random draws each). The neuron needs no labels, so it is a flat line. "All replies" pools every simulated reply for that model (all five behaviours' openers, about 2,500); "Hard" keeps this behaviour's Elicit and Near-miss replies only.

Each panel has its own slider, which sets what share of this behaviour's simulated replies (about 500) the detector flags, ranked by its score. Its four tabs sort every reply into correct positives (flagged, judge positive), false alarms (flagged, judge negative), misses (not flagged, judge positive) and correct negatives (not flagged, judge negative); the counts update as the slider moves, and each tab lists its replies with the highest score first. Precision and recall are computed on the same replies.
